findings.detail: `handbooks/architecture/frontend-boundaries.md` maps the layers as `services/` = I/O and `utils/` = pure logic, with rule 2 placing direct `fetch` in `services/`. `fetchYallaMenu` is a network orchestrator in `utils/` (the module header acknowledges it: "Pure except `fetchYallaMenu`"), and `components/WebScraperTab.tsx:55` supplies the browser `fetch` directly. I am NOT treating this as a blocking violation: the rule's stated rationale is testability, and this PR satisfies it better than the code around it — the I/O is dependency-injected and `tests/unit/yallaMenu.test.ts` exercises the whole fetch path with no network and no DOM, which none of the eight pre-existing `fetch(` calls in this same function can claim. What would make it blocking is I/O *logic* (retry, header, or endpoint decisions) living in the component rather than a one-line fetch adapter. Flagging it so the layer map stays honest as this module grows.
findings.summary: Network I/O lives in `utils/`, and the raw `fetch` reference is in the component

findings.detail: `get()` calls `fetchFn` with no `AbortSignal` and no deadline. `fetch` has no default timeout, so if `kelah.yallaqrcodes.com/api/categories/` accepts the connection and then stalls (captive portal, overloaded origin, DNS-level blackhole), `fetchYallaMenu` never settles: the `catch` in `WebScraperTab.tsx:59` never runs, the documented page-text fallback never fires, and the tab sits at 5% with the last log line `Processing <url>...` and no way to cancel. This is the one failure mode the try/catch design does not actually cover — every other path (non-2xx, CORS refusal, malformed JSON) is handled correctly. The Jina route next to it already guards this server-side with `X-Timeout: 30`.
findings.summary: No timeout on the menu API calls — a hung request never falls back

findings.detail: Every non-deleted item gets its own `/api/items/<id>/` request (correctly so — the comment explains `options_count` is unreliable), six at a time. The real kelah menu is 26 sections, so a few hundred round trips before anything is shown is plausible. `setProgress(40)` only runs after `fetchContent` returns, so the bar stays at 5% and the log stays silent for the entire fetch; a user on a slow connection cannot distinguish "reading 300 items" from "hung". Low rather than medium because the work completes and the success log afterwards is genuinely informative — it would rise if a menu ever pushes this past ~30s.
findings.summary: Per-item detail fan-out gives no progress signal while it runs

findings.detail: `yallaMenuSource` and `yallaMenuText` both declare their return types; `fetchYallaMenu` relies on inference for `{ text, stats, failedDetails }`. `handbooks/language/typescript/type-safety.md` rule 6 asks exported functions to carry explicit return types so a public signature cannot change silently — here, adding or renaming a returned field would propagate into `WebScraperTab.tsx:55`'s destructure without the compiler flagging the contract change.
findings.summary: Exported `fetchYallaMenu` has no explicit return type

findings.detail: `Array.isArray(categories)` / `Array.isArray(items)` validates the container, not the elements, and the result is then asserted into typed arrays. If the platform ever returns `data: [null, …]` or an object per element, `live(items)` / `i.is_deleted` throws a `TypeError` inside `fetchYallaMenu`. The blast radius is genuinely contained — the throw lands in the component's `catch` and the page-text fallback runs with a warning — which is why this is low, not medium. Per `handbooks/language/typescript/type-safety.md` rule 4, external data stays `unknown` until validated.
findings.summary: Third-party JSON cast to `YallaCategory[]` / `YallaItem[]` after an `Array.isArray` check only

findings.detail: `variantPrice` treats a required option's `price` as the FULL price (well-evidenced: ديناميت دجاج 22 → صغير 18 / كبير 22, and pinned by a test), while the add-on line renders the same field as `+${money(o.price ?? 0)}` — a surcharge. Both readings come from one platform field distinguished only by `min_options`. If an optional modifier ever carries full prices the way required ones do, the add-on text hands the model `عسل +37.00` and that wrong figure reaches the Description column of the export. No action needed if the capture confirms the split — recording it so the assumption is visible rather than implicit.
findings.summary: `option.price` is read as a full price for required choices and as a surcharge for add-ons
